subject: Engineering Fundamentals
title: The de Havilland Comet: First Jet Airliner's Fatal Flaw
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The de Havilland Comet: First Jet Airliner's Fatal Flaw.

hook.text: The de Havilland Comet was the world's first jet airliner. In 1954, two of them broke apart in mid-air.

buildup.text: The Comet cruised at 40,000 feet — much higher than propeller planes. Its cabin pressurization cycled with every flight.

discovery.text: Square windows concentrated stress at their corners. Metal fatigue cracks grew from rivet holes near the window edges.

twist.text: Engineers didn't understand pressurization fatigue. The concept of cyclic stress failure in aircraft was essentially unknown.

climax.text: All aircraft now use oval windows. Fatigue testing of pressurized fuselages became mandatory before certification.

punchline.text: Square corners focused stress. Round windows spread it. Lives depended on geometry.

quiz.question: Why did the de Havilland Comet's square windows cause structural failure?
options: Square glass panes shattered more easily at high altitude pressures
Square corners concentrated stress where fatigue cracks grew from rivet holes
The square frames leaked air, causing rapid decompression during flight
